internship.title: API Development Internship
internship.description: An industry-oriented API engineering internship centered on designing, implementing, securing, testing, documenting, and operating a REST-style HTTP service. The program progresses from HTTP semantics and resource modeling into FastAPI architecture, validation, persistence with SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL, authentication and object-level authorization, automated testing and debugging, configuration and observability, performance/resource controls, Docker runtime networking, Git workflow, and one integrated capstone. The selected stack is intentionally explicit rather than implied by the generic internship name, and the capstone keeps frontend work out of scope so the intern can concentrate on API engineering depth.
internship.durationRationale: Approximately 96 hours: guided technical study and design work are combined with practical implementation, seven module-level engineering tasks, test/debug cycles, and a substantial capstone. The duration assumes the intern can already write basic Python and use a terminal; it is not intended as a zero-programming introduction.
prerequisites: Basic Python programming: functions, classes, exceptions, modules, virtual environments, and simple file/package organization.
Basic SQL concepts: tables, primary keys, foreign keys, INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, and transactions.
Basic HTTP knowledge: URLs, request/response, common methods, and JSON.
Comfort using a terminal and installing Python packages with pip.
Basic Git usage: clone, status, add, commit, and branch.
A development machine capable of running Python 3.13+; Docker is required for the capstone orchestration path.
objectives: Design resource-oriented HTTP APIs with deliberate methods, status codes, headers, and JSON contracts.
Build modular FastAPI services using routers, Pydantic schemas, and reusable dependencies.
Persist API data with SQLAlchemy 2.x and PostgreSQL using constraints, transactions, and purposeful indexes.
Implement password-based authentication with bearer JWTs and enforce object-level authorization on protected resources.
Create API tests, diagnose defects, and add regression coverage around security and business invariants.
Manage environment configuration, readiness checks, operational logging, OpenAPI documentation, and Docker Compose networking.
Apply bounded pagination and query design principles to reduce avoidable resource-consumption risks.
Use Git branches, focused commits, code-review evidence, and a documented handoff process for API changes.
Complete and explain one integrated API capstone with architecture, code, tests, security review, and operational guidance.

modules.title: HTTP, Resource Modeling, and API Contracts
modules.description: Establish protocol fluency and a disciplined resource model before implementing framework code.
objectives: Interpret HTTP request/response semantics and choose methods and status codes deliberately.
Model resources and URI structures that make client intent and authorization context explicit.
Define stable JSON representations and safe error contracts.

lessons.title: HTTP as the API Contract
lessons.description: Build a precise mental model of an API request/response before touching framework code.
learningObjectives: Explain the client, origin server, resource, representation, and request/response concepts in HTTP.
Distinguish method semantics from application-specific endpoint behavior.
Interpret status codes and headers when diagnosing an API interaction.

notes.text: HTTP semantics are the first contract

HTTP is a stateless application-level request/response protocol. The method, target URI, selected representation, headers, status code, and content together communicate intent and result. Framework routes are implementations of those semantics, not replacements for them.

items: GET is safe; POST is not safe and is commonly used for creation or actions.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics, although an application must still define correct resource behavior.
Use status codes deliberately: 2xx for successful handling, 4xx when the client request cannot be accepted, and 5xx when the server fails to fulfill a valid request.

notes.text: Do not overload status codes to encode arbitrary business states when the HTTP meaning becomes misleading. Keep domain state in the response representation.

practicals.title: Inspect a real API exchange
practicals.description: Use curl against a public HTTP endpoint you control or a local service to identify method, URI, headers, status, and content.
steps: Start a local FastAPI service that exposes a GET /health/live endpoint.
Run `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/live` and record the status line, selected response headers, and body.
Repeat with a nonexistent path and compare the status code and response body.
Explain which parts of the exchange are protocol-level semantics and which are application-specific.
practicals.output: The first request should return a successful 2xx response with the service-defined JSON body. The second should return a 4xx response because the requested resource does not exist.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes HTTP statelessness?
options: The server must never store data.
Each request can be interpreted without relying on a prior connection state for its semantics.
Clients may only send one request per connection.
Every request must contain a session cookie.
quiz.answer: Each request can be interpreted without relying on a prior connection state for its semantics.
quiz.explanation: HTTP semantics are defined so a request can be understood independently; applications may add state mechanisms such as cookies or tokens.

summary: HTTP semantics are the foundation for predictable API clients.
Method meaning, status codes, and resource identity should be designed together.

lessons.title: Resource Modeling, URIs, and Methods
lessons.description: Turn business nouns into resource-oriented paths and choose methods according to HTTP semantics.
learningObjectives: Design resource-oriented URI paths for collections and individual resources.
Choose methods for retrieval, creation, replacement, and deletion based on semantics.
Recognize action-style endpoints that should be justified rather than added by habit.

notes.text: A useful API model starts with resources: users, projects, issues, and similar durable entities. Collection routes such as /projects and item routes such as /projects/42 make the target resource explicit.

items: Prefer plural collection nouns for stable resource collections.
Use path parameters for resource identity and query parameters for filtering, sorting, and pagination.
An action endpoint can be appropriate when the operation is not naturally represented as changing one resource, but the semantics should be documented explicitly.

practicals.title: Model an issue-tracking resource tree
practicals.description: Design a URI map for users, projects, and issues and justify each path.
steps: Define collection and item URIs for users and projects.
Nest issues under a project when the project is required context for authorization.
For each route, record its method, request body, response status, and authorization requirement.
Review the design for ambiguous or duplicate identifiers.
practicals.solution:
GET    /users/me
POST   /projects
GET    /projects
GET    /projects/{project_id}
POST   /projects/{project_id}/issues
GET    /projects/{project_id}/issues
PATCH  /projects/{project_id}/issues/{issue_id}
practicals.output: The result is a resource hierarchy where project_id provides security context for issue access.

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate about Resource Modeling, URIs, and Methods?
options: The topic can be ignored in a real API.
The topic should be applied consistently with the API contract and taught implementation.
The topic only matters to frontend styling.
The topic replaces database constraints.
quiz.answer: The topic should be applied consistently with the API contract and taught implementation.
quiz.explanation: The lesson is about Resource Modeling, URIs, and Methods; its value is in applying the concept consistently within the API design and implementation.

summary: Resource-oriented paths make API behavior discoverable.
Query parameters are a good fit for collection shaping; path parameters identify resources.

lessons.title: Representations, JSON, and Error Contracts
lessons.description: Design stable JSON request and response shapes, including predictable error responses.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a resource and its representation.
Define fields that are stable enough for clients to depend on.
Design error responses that are useful to clients without exposing sensitive internals.

notes.text: A representation is data transferred to or from a client; it is not necessarily a direct dump of a database row. API schemas should intentionally expose the public contract.

items: Keep identifiers, timestamps, and enum values consistent across versions.
Use response models to control which fields leave the service.
Return actionable validation errors while avoiding stack traces, database messages, or secrets in production responses.

quiz.question: Why use a dedicated response model instead of returning a database entity directly?
options: It makes the database faster.
It prevents accidental exposure of internal fields and defines the public contract.
It removes the need for validation.
It automatically authenticates the client.
quiz.answer: It prevents accidental exposure of internal fields and defines the public contract.
quiz.explanation: A response model creates an explicit boundary between persistence data and externally exposed fields.

summary: Public response shapes should be designed separately from persistence models.
Error responses are part of the API contract and need the same discipline as successful responses.

POST   /projects

notes.text: FastAPI can generate OpenAPI documentation from route declarations, parameter types, and Pydantic models. APIRouter lets an application group related endpoints and include them under consistent prefixes and tags.

lessons.title: Pydantic Models and Boundary Validation
lessons.description: Treat incoming JSON as untrusted data and use typed schemas to validate it at the API boundary.
learningObjectives: Define Pydantic models for request and response payloads.
Use field constraints and enums/literals to reject malformed requests before business logic.
Explain why validation belongs at the transport boundary as well as in the data layer.

notes.text: FastAPI uses Pydantic models to validate JSON bodies. The model is a contract: it states which fields are accepted, their types, and constraints such as length or allowed values.

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class IssueCreate(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    status: Literal["open", "in_progress", "closed"] = "open"
Validation is not a substitute for database constraints. A unique email, foreign key, or transactional invariant belongs in the database too.

quiz.question: Which control best prevents an issue status outside the supported states?
options: A SQL comment
A Pydantic Literal or enum validation rule
A longer URL
A response model only
quiz.answer: A Pydantic Literal or enum validation rule
quiz.explanation: The input schema can reject values outside the declared domain before application logic runs.

summary: Pydantic schemas define the API boundary.
Use model constraints for shape and range; use database constraints for integrity.

lessons.title: Dependencies and Shared Request Context
lessons.description: Use FastAPI dependencies to share sessions, authentication, and resource-loading logic.
learningObjectives: Create dependency functions that provide request-scoped resources.
Chain dependencies so protected routes receive an authenticated user or authorized resource.
Keep route handlers small by moving cross-cutting request logic into dependencies.

notes.text: Dependencies are part of FastAPI’s request processing model. A dependency can itself depend on other dependencies, allowing a route to declare what context it needs.

items: Database sessions should be closed after the request.
Authentication and authorization dependencies should return safe failures rather than leaking internal exceptions.
Resource lookup and ownership checks are particularly valuable as reusable dependencies for APIs with nested resources.

tasks.title: Bound a paginated collection endpoint
tasks.description: Extend a collection endpoint with bounded pagination, optional owner filtering, and deterministic ordering.
tasks.problemStatement: GET /projects returns every record. Add page, page_size, optional owner_id, and order parameters. page_size must be between 1 and 100. Apply limits at the database query, not after loading all rows.
objectives: validate query parameters
apply offset and limit in SQLAlchemy
make ordering deterministic
tasks.hint: Apply filters and ordering to the select statement, then use offset/limit. Add a stable tie-breaker such as id.
tasks.solutionCode:
from typing import Literal
from fastapi import APIRouter, Query, Depends
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

@router.get("/projects")
def list_projects(
    page: int = Query(1, ge=1),
    page_size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100),
    owner_id: int | None = Query(None, ge=1),
    order: Literal["asc", "desc"] = "desc",
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
):
    stmt = select(Project)
    if owner_id is not None:
        stmt = stmt.where(Project.owner_id == owner_id)
    primary = Project.created_at.asc() if order == "asc" else Project.created_at.desc()
    stmt = stmt.order_by(primary, Project.id.desc())
    stmt = stmt.offset((page - 1) * page_size).limit(page_size)
    rows = list(db.scalars(stmt))
    return {"page": page, "page_size": page_size, "items": rows}
tasks.solutionExplanation: Validation bounds the request, filtering stays in SQL, and the id tie-breaker prevents unstable ordering when timestamps match. Pagination at the query level avoids loading the full table into application memory.

deliverables: Tests for page bounds, deterministic ordering, and filter behavior
modules.assessment: Review for correct boundary validation and database-level pagination rather than in-memory slicing.

modules.title: Persistence, Integrity, and Query Design
modules.description: Give API endpoints a reliable relational persistence layer and teach the intern to reason about transactions and query cost.
objectives: Map API domain concepts to relational tables and relationships.
Use constraints and transaction handling to protect data integrity.
Design predictable paginated queries and purposeful indexes.

lessons.title: SQLAlchemy 2.x ORM Mapping and Sessions
lessons.description: Map domain entities to relational tables and manage request-scoped sessions correctly.
learningObjectives: Define declarative models with typed Mapped attributes.
Explain identity, relationships, and session lifecycle in SQLAlchemy 2.x.
Choose when to commit, refresh, or roll back a transaction.

notes.text: The SQLAlchemy ORM maps Python objects to relational tables. A Session coordinates object state and database transactions; it is not a global cache and should not be shared across unrelated concurrent requests.

items: One request can typically use one short-lived Session.
Commit when an atomic unit of business work succeeds; roll back on integrity failures.
Refresh an object after commit when generated database values are needed immediately.

practicals.title: Implement an ownership relationship
practicals.description: Create User and Project models with a foreign key and back-populated relationship.
steps: Define a users table with a primary-key id.
Define projects.owner_id as a non-null foreign key to users.id.
Add SQLAlchemy relationships on both models.
Create the tables in a disposable test database and insert one user/project pair.
Query the user and access the related projects through the ORM relationship.
practicals.solution:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True, nullable=False)
    projects: Mapped[list["Project"]] = relationship(back_populates="owner")

class Project(Base):
    __tablename__ = "projects"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    owner_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"), nullable=False)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120), nullable=False)
    owner: Mapped[User] = relationship(back_populates="projects")
practicals.output: The database schema contains a real foreign key and the ORM exposes a bidirectional relationship.

lessons.title: Constraints, Transactions, and Integrity
lessons.description: Make invalid states hard to create by combining database constraints with explicit transaction handling.
learningObjectives: Use primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and not-null constraints appropriately.
Handle transaction failures with rollback and safe client-facing errors.
Explain why application-only checks can race under concurrent requests.

notes.text: Database constraints are authoritative because multiple application instances can race. A pre-check such as “does this email exist?” is useful for user feedback but cannot replace the database unique constraint.
Never leave a failed SQLAlchemy Session in a transaction state and then keep using it. Roll back before issuing subsequent work.

quiz.question: Why is a database unique constraint still needed when the API checks for an existing email first?
options: It improves JSON formatting.
Concurrent requests can both pass the pre-check before either insert commits.
It is only needed for backups.
It replaces authentication.
quiz.answer: Concurrent requests can both pass the pre-check before either insert commits.
quiz.explanation: The database is the final arbiter of uniqueness under concurrency.

summary: Constraints protect integrity across concurrent application instances.
Rollback is required to restore a usable transaction state after an error.

lessons.title: Query Design, Indexes, and Pagination
lessons.description: Shape SQL queries for the API’s access patterns and use indexes that support those queries.
learningObjectives: Write SQLAlchemy select statements with filtering, ordering, and pagination.
Explain what an index can and cannot optimize.
Use composite indexes that reflect common query predicates and ordering patterns.

notes.text: Indexes accelerate specific lookup patterns at the cost of storage and write maintenance. An index is useful when its leading columns match the query predicate/order pattern the database can exploit.

stmt = (
    select(Project)
    .where(Project.owner_id == owner_id)
    .order_by(Project.created_at.desc(), Project.id.desc())
    .offset(offset)
    .limit(page_size)
)

items: Do not add indexes without a query need.
Measure slow queries before and after changes.
Use a deterministic order for paginated APIs; identical sort keys need a tie-breaker.

tasks.title: Enforce a transactional project invariant
tasks.description: Protect project creation from duplicate names per owner using both application logic and a database constraint.
tasks.problemStatement: Two requests from the same owner may attempt to create the same project name concurrently. Implement the service and schema changes needed so at most one succeeds, with the losing request receiving HTTP 409.
objectives: define the unique constraint
handle IntegrityError with rollback
write a regression test for conflict behavior
requirements: PostgreSQL or SQLite for unit-level test
tasks.hint: The database constraint is the final guarantee; the service should translate its violation into a conflict response.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The constraint provides concurrency-safe uniqueness. The rollback clears the failed transaction state, and HTTP 409 communicates a resource-state conflict without leaking raw database errors.

modules.title: Authentication, Authorization, and API Security
modules.description: Build identity and access-control mechanisms directly into API endpoints, then review them against API-specific threat categories.
objectives: Implement password-based authentication and JWT bearer token validation.
Enforce object-level authorization on every protected resource path.
Use OWASP API risks to identify security controls and regression tests.

lessons.title: Authentication with Passwords and JWT Bearer Tokens
lessons.description: Implement a standards-aligned authentication flow while keeping password handling and token validation explicit.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between authentication and authorization.
Hash passwords rather than storing plaintext secrets.
Validate JWT signature, subject, and expiry before trusting identity claims.

notes.text: Authentication answers “who are you?” Authorization answers “what may you do?” They are related but distinct controls.

items: Password verification should compare against a salted password hash produced by a suitable password-hashing library.
JWT validation must verify the signature and registered claims such as expiry.
Signing secrets must come from secure configuration, not source code.

notes.text: Bearer tokens must be treated as credentials. Never log them, embed them in URLs, or commit them to source control.

practicals.title: Protect a current-user endpoint
practicals.description: Add OAuth2 password flow token issuance and a dependency that returns the authenticated user.
steps: Add a password-hashing dependency and an authentication service.
Create POST /auth/token that accepts username/password and returns a bearer token.
Create a dependency that decodes and validates the token and loads the user.
Protect GET /users/me with the dependency.
Verify that invalid credentials return 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header.
practicals.output: A valid access token allows GET /users/me; invalid credentials are rejected with 401.

options: The topic can be ignored in a real API.
The topic should be applied consistently with the API contract and taught implementation.

lessons.title: Authorization and Object-Level Access Control
lessons.description: Prevent broken object-level authorization by checking ownership or permission on the requested resource itself.
learningObjectives: Explain broken object-level authorization (BOLA) as an API risk.
Implement resource lookup plus ownership validation before returning or mutating objects.
Differentiate 401 authentication failures from 403 authorization failures.

notes.text: An endpoint such as GET /projects/42 must not infer access from the existence of project 42. It must evaluate whether the authenticated principal is allowed to access that resource.
Do not accept a client-supplied owner_id as proof of authorization. Authorization must use trusted server-side identity and policy data.

quiz.question: What is the core problem in a BOLA vulnerability?
options: A client can access an object by changing its identifier without an authorization check.
A server returns JSON.
A route uses HTTPS.
A database uses indexes.
quiz.answer: A client can access an object by changing its identifier without an authorization check.
quiz.explanation: BOLA occurs when object-level permissions are not enforced for the object selected by a user-controlled identifier.

summary: Resource access checks belong at the point where the resource is resolved.
Authorization must be applied consistently to reads and writes.

lessons.title: API Security Risks and Secure Error Handling
lessons.description: Use OWASP API Security Top 10 concepts to guide threat modeling and secure endpoint behavior.
learningObjectives: Map common API threats to concrete controls.
Identify excessive data exposure, unrestricted resource consumption, and broken function-level authorization risks.
Design errors and logs that support troubleshooting without disclosing secrets.

notes.text: The OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights recurring API-specific weaknesses. Interns should treat the list as a threat-modeling aid rather than a checklist that proves a service is secure.

items: BOLA requires object-level access checks.
Broken authentication requires robust credential and session/token handling.
Unrestricted resource consumption calls for bounded pagination, payload sizes, timeouts, and rate-limit strategies appropriate to the service.
Security misconfiguration includes unsafe defaults, overly permissive CORS, debug exposure, and missing secure headers or transport controls.

notes.text: A secure error message is actionable for the client but not a stack trace, SQL statement, credential, or secret.

The topic only matters to frontend styling.

Security requirements should be tested as regression behavior, not merely documented.

tasks.title: Add request correlation to safe logs
tasks.description: Add a request identifier to logs without recording authentication secrets.
tasks.problemStatement: Every request should have a correlation id. Add middleware that accepts a client-supplied X-Request-ID only when it matches a conservative format, otherwise generates a UUID. Log the method, path, status, and request id at completion. Do not log Authorization headers or request bodies.
objectives: create a safe correlation identifier
include it in response headers and logs
avoid sensitive fields
tasks.hint: Treat the incoming header as untrusted input and validate its format before accepting it.
tasks.solutionCode:
import logging
import re
import uuid
from fastapi import Request

logger = logging.getLogger("api.request")
SAFE_ID = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$")

@app.middleware("http")
async def correlation_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    candidate = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID", "")
    request_id = candidate if SAFE_ID.fullmatch(candidate) else str(uuid.uuid4())
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = request_id
    logger.info("request_complete request_id=%s method=%s path=%s status=%s", request_id, request.method, request.url.path, response.status_code)
    return response
tasks.solutionExplanation: The middleware produces a bounded correlation id, propagates it in the response, and records only operational metadata. It deliberately excludes credentials, request bodies, and bearer tokens.

modules.assessment: Security review must confirm that the logging line cannot accidentally serialize secrets or credentials.

project.heading: Build a Secure Issue-Tracking API with FastAPI and PostgreSQL
project.name: Secure Issue-Tracking API
project.description: Build a complete authenticated REST-style API for managing projects and issues. The service is intended for a small internal engineering workflow: users register, authenticate with a bearer token, create projects they own, and create/update issues inside those projects. The project gives the intern one coherent system in which HTTP design, validation, persistence, access control, testing, observability, documentation, containerized runtime setup, and engineering workflow all interact.
project.problemStatement: A small engineering team needs a reliable API for tracking projects and issues without allowing users to read or modify resources they do not own. The service must expose a clear HTTP contract, validate input, enforce relational integrity, authenticate users, authorize each protected resource, provide actionable operational health endpoints, remain testable, and run reproducibly with PostgreSQL in containers.
objectives: Design a resource-oriented API with explicit request and response contracts.
Implement registration and JWT bearer authentication with secure password hashing.
Enforce project ownership and parent-resource authorization for issue operations.
Persist data with PostgreSQL-compatible SQLAlchemy mappings and integrity constraints.
Add API-level regression tests for health, authentication, validation, and authorization behavior.
Expose operational health endpoints and environment-driven configuration.
Run the service with Docker Compose and document the deployment boundary between local learning and production hardening.
requirements: FastAPI 0.141.1 and Uvicorn 0.52.4 for the researched runtime baseline.
Pydantic 2.13.5 and pydantic-settings 2.15.0 for request/configuration models.
SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 with Psycopg 3.3.5 for PostgreSQL access.
pwdlib 0.3.1 with Argon2 support for password hashing.
pytest 9.1.1 and HTTPX-compatible FastAPI testing support.
Docker Compose for reproducible local orchestration.
A Git repository for versioned change history and review.
features: User registration accepts an email address and password meeting the defined length rule, hashes the password, and returns only a public user representation.
Token issuance authenticates the submitted credentials and returns a short-lived bearer token containing the user subject and expiry claim.
Current-user endpoint returns the authenticated user without exposing password hashes or token material.
Project creation enforces a per-owner unique name using both an application-level conflict translation and a database unique constraint.
Project listing returns only projects owned by the authenticated user and uses deterministic newest-first ordering.
Project retrieval, update, and deletion verify that the authenticated user owns the selected project before allowing access.
Issue creation requires an owned project and validates title length, description length, and status values.
Issue listing is scoped to the selected owned project.
Issue updates validate the patch payload and ensure the issue belongs to the requested project before mutation.
Liveness and readiness endpoints separate process health from database availability.
OpenAPI is generated from the route and schema definitions and is available through FastAPI documentation endpoints.

testPrinciples: Add regression coverage when defects are fixed.

securityReview: Passwords are hashed and never stored or returned in plaintext.
JWT signing secrets are supplied through environment configuration and are not hard-coded in application source.
Protected resources require a validated bearer token.
Project and issue access is checked against trusted server-side ownership data.
Request data is validated through Pydantic field constraints.
Collection page size is bounded in the taught pagination pattern to reduce resource-consumption risk.
Health and request logs do not intentionally include passwords, bearer tokens, or signing secrets.
The example Compose secret is for local development only and must be replaced before any shared environment.

Production deployment should add HTTPS/TLS termination, managed secret storage, database migrations, rate limiting where required, dependency update policy, and more complete authorization policy testing.
performanceGuidance: Apply pagination at the database query instead of loading full collections into Python.
Use deterministic ordering with a tie-breaker for stable page contents.
Create indexes only for demonstrated access patterns and verify with database plans/measurements.
For very large datasets, evaluate keyset/cursor pagination instead of large OFFSET values.
Do not claim performance benchmarks until the service is measured under a defined workload.

deploymentGuidance.local: Docker Compose runs PostgreSQL and the API on the same Compose network; the database is addressed as `db` inside the API container.
deploymentGuidance.productionBoundary: The capstone is an educational reference and not a drop-in production deployment. Production should use managed secrets, formal migrations, a reverse proxy/TLS boundary, externalized PostgreSQL, monitoring, backups, explicit resource limits, and tested rollback procedures.
deploymentGuidance.rollback: Treat database migrations and application releases as separate rollback concerns. Backward-compatible database changes reduce deployment coupling.

checks: Confirm Authorization header is `Bearer <token>`.
Confirm JWT secret in the running process matches the one used to sign the token.

# API Development Internship Capstone

This service is a small authenticated issue-tracking API. Users can register and obtain JWT access tokens. Authenticated users can create projects they own and create issues within those projects. Project membership is owner-only in this capstone so that object-level authorization is explicit and easy to audit.

## Local setup

1. Create a Python 3.13+ virtual environment.
2. Run `pip install -e ".[test]"`.
3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and replace the development secret.
4. Start PostgreSQL with `docker compose up -d db`.
5. Start the API with `uvicorn app.main:app --reload`.
6. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

## Container setup

Run `docker compose up --build`. The API waits for the database health check before the container starts.

## Tests

Run `pytest`. The test suite uses SQLite in memory for fast unit/API coverage; PostgreSQL-specific integration should still be executed against the Compose database before deployment.

## Security notes

Do not use the example JWT secret in any shared or production environment. Tokens, passwords, and connection credentials are not logged. Access-control checks are performed on the requested project resource rather than trusting an identifier supplied by the client.

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

import jwt
from jwt.exceptions import PyJWTError

from app.core.config import settings
from app.db import get_db
from app.models import Project, User


oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/auth/token")
credentials_error = HTTPException(
    status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
    detail="Invalid authentication credentials",
    headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
)


def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme), db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> User:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, settings.jwt_secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
        subject = payload.get("sub")
        if subject is None:
            raise credentials_error
        user_id = int(subject)
    except (PyJWTError, ValueError, TypeError):
        raise credentials_error

    user = db.get(User, user_id)
    if user is None:
        raise credentials_error
    return user


def require_project_owner(project_id: int, current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user), db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> Project:
    project = db.scalar(select(Project).where(Project.id == project_id))
    if project is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Project not found")
    if project.owner_id != current_user.id:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")
    return project

from fastapi import HTTPException, status
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from app.core.security import hash_password, verify_password
from app.models import Issue, Project, User
from app.schemas import IssueCreate, IssuePatch, ProjectCreate, UserCreate


def create_user(db: Session, payload: UserCreate) -> User:
    user = User(email=payload.email.lower(), password_hash=hash_password(payload.password))
    db.add(user)
    try:
        db.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        db.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Email already registered")
    db.refresh(user)
    return user


def authenticate_user(db: Session, email: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user = db.scalar(select(User).where(User.email == email.lower()))
    if user is None or not verify_password(password, user.password_hash):
        return None
    return user


def create_project(db: Session, owner: User, payload: ProjectCreate) -> Project:
    project = Project(owner_id=owner.id, name=payload.name.strip(), description=payload.description)
    db.add(project)
    try:
        db.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        db.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Project name already exists for this owner")
    db.refresh(project)
    return project


def create_issue(db: Session, project: Project, payload: IssueCreate) -> Issue:
    issue = Issue(project_id=project.id, title=payload.title.strip(), description=payload.description, status=payload.status)
    db.add(issue)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(issue)
    return issue


def patch_issue(db: Session, issue: Issue, payload: IssuePatch) -> Issue:
    data = payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    for field, value in data.items():
        if field in {"title", "description", "status"} and value is None and field != "description":
            raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail=f"{field} cannot be null")
        if field == "title" and isinstance(value, str):
            value = value.strip()
            if not value:
                raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="title cannot be empty")
        setattr(issue, field, value)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(issue)
    return issue

A client registers through /auth/register, then submits credentials to /auth/token. The token contains the user id in the subject claim and an expiry. Protected routes decode the token, load the user, and then authorize the requested project resource. Project and issue data are persisted through a SQLAlchemy session connected to PostgreSQL. Pydantic response models serialize only public fields. Health endpoints provide liveness and database-backed readiness signals. The automated test suite exercises the HTTP boundary with an isolated SQLite database.
dataFlow: Registration: Client -> POST /auth/register -> Pydantic UserCreate -> password hash -> User insert -> UserPublic response
Login: Client -> POST /auth/token (form) -> credential lookup -> password verification -> JWT -> client
Project read: Client + Bearer -> auth dependency -> owner dependency -> SQLAlchemy project query -> ownership check -> ProjectPublic response
Issue update: Client + Bearer -> project ownership check -> issue lookup scoped by project_id + issue_id -> validation -> transaction commit -> IssuePublic response
project.finalExplanation: This capstone demonstrates API development as a complete engineering discipline rather than as route writing alone. The contract begins with HTTP and resource design. FastAPI and Pydantic turn the contract into typed endpoints. SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL enforce persistence and integrity. Security dependencies establish identity and object-level authorization. pytest converts critical behavior into repeatable evidence. Docker Compose makes the runtime topology reproducible. OpenAPI makes the surface inspectable by both humans and tooling. The most important implementation decision is to keep authorization tied to server-side resource ownership rather than trusting identifiers or client-provided ownership claims. The README distinguishes local educational conveniences from production requirements so the intern learns where a reference implementation ends and a real deployment process begins.

testPrinciples: Add regression coverage when defects are fixed.

securityReview: Passwords are hashed and never stored or returned in plaintext.
JWT signing secrets are supplied through environment configuration and are not hard-coded in application source.
Protected resources require a validated bearer token.
Project and issue access is checked against trusted server-side ownership data.
Request data is validated through Pydantic field constraints.
Collection page size is bounded in the taught pagination pattern to reduce resource-consumption risk.
Health and request logs do not intentionally include passwords, bearer tokens, or signing secrets.
The example Compose secret is for local development only and must be replaced before any shared environment.

Production deployment should add HTTPS/TLS termination, managed secret storage, database migrations, rate limiting where required, dependency update policy, and more complete authorization policy testing.
performanceGuidance: Apply pagination at the database query instead of loading full collections into Python.
Use deterministic ordering with a tie-breaker for stable page contents.
Create indexes only for demonstrated access patterns and verify with database plans/measurements.
For very large datasets, evaluate keyset/cursor pagination instead of large OFFSET values.
Do not claim performance benchmarks until the service is measured under a defined workload.

deploymentGuidance.local: Docker Compose runs PostgreSQL and the API on the same Compose network; the database is addressed as `db` inside the API container.
deploymentGuidance.productionBoundary: The capstone is an educational reference and not a drop-in production deployment. Production should use managed secrets, formal migrations, a reverse proxy/TLS boundary, externalized PostgreSQL, monitoring, backups, explicit resource limits, and tested rollback procedures.
deploymentGuidance.rollback: Treat database migrations and application releases as separate rollback concerns. Backward-compatible database changes reduce deployment coupling.

fileWiseSolution.purpose: Explains how to run, test, inspect, and operate the capstone.
fileWiseSolution.explanation: The README is deliberately operational: an intern should be able to reproduce the local environment, understand the HTTP contract, and know where production hardening would be required.
fileWiseSolution.code:
# API Development Internship Capstone

This service is a small authenticated issue-tracking API. Users can register and obtain JWT access tokens. Authenticated users can create projects they own and create issues within those projects. Project membership is owner-only in this capstone so that object-level authorization is explicit and easy to audit.

## Local setup

1. Create a Python 3.13+ virtual environment.
2. Run `pip install -e ".[test]"`.
3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and replace the development secret.
4. Start PostgreSQL with `docker compose up -d db`.
5. Start the API with `uvicorn app.main:app --reload`.
6. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

## Container setup

Run `docker compose up --build`. The API waits for the database health check before the container starts.

## Tests

Run `pytest`. The test suite uses SQLite in memory for fast unit/API coverage; PostgreSQL-specific integration should still be executed against the Compose database before deployment.

## Security notes

Do not use the example JWT secret in any shared or production environment. Tokens, passwords, and connection credentials are not logged. Access-control checks are performed on the requested project resource rather than trusting an identifier supplied by the client.

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

import jwt
from jwt.exceptions import PyJWTError

from app.core.config import settings
from app.db import get_db
from app.models import Project, User


oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/auth/token")
credentials_error = HTTPException(
    status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
    detail="Invalid authentication credentials",
    headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
)


def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme), db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> User:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, settings.jwt_secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
        subject = payload.get("sub")
        if subject is None:
            raise credentials_error
        user_id = int(subject)
    except (PyJWTError, ValueError, TypeError):
        raise credentials_error

    user = db.get(User, user_id)
    if user is None:
        raise credentials_error
    return user


def require_project_owner(project_id: int, current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user), db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> Project:
    project = db.scalar(select(Project).where(Project.id == project_id))
    if project is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Project not found")
    if project.owner_id != current_user.id:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")
    return project

fileWiseSolution.explanation: Keeping business rules outside the router layer makes them easier to test and reuse while preserving transaction boundaries in the service functions.

from fastapi import HTTPException, status
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from app.core.security import hash_password, verify_password
from app.models import Issue, Project, User
from app.schemas import IssueCreate, IssuePatch, ProjectCreate, UserCreate


def create_user(db: Session, payload: UserCreate) -> User:
    user = User(email=payload.email.lower(), password_hash=hash_password(payload.password))
    db.add(user)
    try:
        db.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        db.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Email already registered")
    db.refresh(user)
    return user


def authenticate_user(db: Session, email: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user = db.scalar(select(User).where(User.email == email.lower()))
    if user is None or not verify_password(password, user.password_hash):
        return None
    return user


def create_project(db: Session, owner: User, payload: ProjectCreate) -> Project:
    project = Project(owner_id=owner.id, name=payload.name.strip(), description=payload.description)
    db.add(project)
    try:
        db.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        db.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Project name already exists for this owner")
    db.refresh(project)
    return project


def create_issue(db: Session, project: Project, payload: IssueCreate) -> Issue:
    issue = Issue(project_id=project.id, title=payload.title.strip(), description=payload.description, status=payload.status)
    db.add(issue)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(issue)
    return issue


def patch_issue(db: Session, issue: Issue, payload: IssuePatch) -> Issue:
    data = payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    for field, value in data.items():
        if field in {"title", "description", "status"} and value is None and field != "description":
            raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail=f"{field} cannot be null")
        if field == "title" and isinstance(value, str):
            value = value.strip()
            if not value:
                raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="title cannot be empty")
        setattr(issue, field, value)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(issue)
    return issue

from tests.test_projects import register_and_token


def test_issue_lifecycle(client):
    token = register_and_token(client, "issue-owner@example.test")
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}

    project_response = client.post("/projects", headers=headers, json={"name": "Issue Project", "description": "Track work"})
    project_id = project_response.json()["id"]

    created = client.post(
        f"/projects/{project_id}/issues",
        headers=headers,
        json={"title": "Fix validation", "description": "Add input validation", "status": "open"},
    )
    assert created.status_code == 201
    issue_id = created.json()["id"]

    updated = client.patch(
        f"/projects/{project_id}/issues/{issue_id}",
        headers=headers,
        json={"status": "closed"},
    )
    assert updated.status_code == 200
    assert updated.json()["status"] == "closed"


def test_invalid_patch_is_rejected(client):
    token = register_and_token(client, "validation-owner@example.test")
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
    project_id = client.post("/projects", headers=headers, json={"name": "Validation", "description": ""}).json()["id"]
    issue_id = client.post(
        f"/projects/{project_id}/issues",
        headers=headers,
        json={"title": "Valid", "description": "", "status": "open"},
    ).json()["id"]

    response = client.patch(
        f"/projects/{project_id}/issues/{issue_id}",
        headers=headers,
        json={"title": ""},
    )
    assert response.status_code in {422, 400}

finalProject.howItWorks: At startup the process reads typed settings and optionally creates development tables when APP_CREATE_TABLES=true. FastAPI registers routers and exposes OpenAPI metadata. A client registers through /auth/register, then submits credentials to /auth/token. The token contains the user id in the subject claim and an expiry. Protected routes decode the token, load the user, and then authorize the requested project resource. Project and issue data are persisted through a SQLAlchemy session connected to PostgreSQL. Pydantic response models serialize only public fields. Health endpoints provide liveness and database-backed readiness signals. The automated test suite exercises the HTTP boundary with an isolated SQLite database.
dataFlow: Registration: Client -> POST /auth/register -> Pydantic UserCreate -> password hash -> User insert -> UserPublic response
Login: Client -> POST /auth/token (form) -> credential lookup -> password verification -> JWT -> client
Project read: Client + Bearer -> auth dependency -> owner dependency -> SQLAlchemy project query -> ownership check -> ProjectPublic response
Issue update: Client + Bearer -> project ownership check -> issue lookup scoped by project_id + issue_id -> validation -> transaction commit -> IssuePublic response
finalProject.finalExplanation: This capstone demonstrates API development as a complete engineering discipline rather than as route writing alone. The contract begins with HTTP and resource design. FastAPI and Pydantic turn the contract into typed endpoints. SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL enforce persistence and integrity. Security dependencies establish identity and object-level authorization. pytest converts critical behavior into repeatable evidence. Docker Compose makes the runtime topology reproducible. OpenAPI makes the surface inspectable by both humans and tooling. The most important implementation decision is to keep authorization tied to server-side resource ownership rather than trusting identifiers or client-provided ownership claims. The README distinguishes local educational conveniences from production requirements so the intern learns where a reference implementation ends and a real deployment process begins.
